Executive Summary Puerto Rico’s year-round high temperatures and humidity create a persistent and growing demand for cooling, especially in residential, commercial, and institutional buildings. This demand significantly contributes to peak electricity loads, primarily driven by widespread reliance on air-conditioning systems that operate inefficiently in many buildings that rely on electricity intensive vapor-compression cooling. The island’s dependence on an aging, import- fueled energy grid makes supplying electricity for cooling expensive and unreliable and increases the island’s vulnerability to disruptions, particularly during extreme weather events like hurricanes. As a potential solution to reduce these vulnerabilities, this study evaluates a novel seawater air conditioning (SWAC) system hydrogeologically connected to cold seawater via inland wells as an alternative to conventional air conditioning. The proposed system, called geologic seawater air conditioning (GeoSWAC), leverages inland wells hydrologically connected to deep, cold seawater through permeable subsurface formations, eliminating a refrigeration cycle to produce cooling.
